title: Cracking the Long-Period Radio Transient Mystery
hook: Some cosmic signals pulse every hour or so — far too slow for the usual suspects. Astronomers traced one to a white dwarf feeding off its companion star.
key_points: 'Long-period radio transients' repeat on timescales of minutes to hours that puzzled astronomers.
Using Australia's ASKAP radio telescope, researchers tied one to a white dwarf–red dwarf binary.
The dense white dwarf siphons material off its red dwarf companion.
As that stolen matter spirals in, the system emits radio waves and X-rays every ~1.4 hours.
It pins a baffling class of signals to a concrete, ordinary stellar mechanism.
content_html: For years, astronomers have puzzled over "long-period radio transients" — sources that flash in radio waves but repeat far too slowly, on the order of an hour, to fit the usual fast-spinning neutron-star story. What kind of object pulses on that timescale?
extra_html: Using Australia's ASKAP radio telescope, researchers traced one such signal to a rare stellar duo: a dense white dwarf locked with a red dwarf companion, relentlessly pulling material off it. As the stolen matter spirals inward, the system unleashes radio waves and X-rays roughly every 1.4 hours. Reported by ScienceDaily, the find acts as a kind of "Rosetta stone" — pinning a mysterious class of slow cosmic signals to a concrete binary-star mechanism rather than an exotic unknown. It's a satisfying example of how a single well-characterized system can decode a whole category of puzzling observations.

related.hook: When a giant star dies, its core collapses and its outer layers blast away in a supernova that can briefly outshine an entire galaxy — leaving behind something extraordinary.

flashcards.prompt: What did astronomers find behind one long-period radio transient?
flashcards.back_html: A binary star system: a dense white dwarf siphoning matter from a red dwarf companion. The infalling material drives bursts of radio waves and X-rays every ~1.4 hours.

flashcards.prompt: What made long-period radio transients so puzzling?

choices.text: They repeat far more slowly than typical cosmic radio sources
They can only be seen from the southern hemisphere

flashcards.explanation_html: Most pulsing radio sources cycle in seconds or less; these repeated on the scale of minutes to hours, which didn't fit the usual neutron-star explanations — hence the mystery.
